audio_caption: The clip starts with dialogue between two speakers, identified as Zach and Steve, presumably male. Steve makes a reference to a previous video where they explained how "refraction in the atmosphere" was the solution to problems with flat earth models, using a conversational and informative tone. Then, they encourage listeners to watch the previous video. A brief, slightly electronic musical interlude then plays.

The audio begins with a male speaker announcing the intention to explain star trails on the flat Earth model. He refers to a previous video and suggests that many people believe that refraction doesn't account for the sunrise and sunset and they think refraction would make the sun rise up instead of down. A distinct "boom" sound abruptly ends the audio clip.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker clarifying, "What we did was add the atmosphere to the flat Earth model in Cinema 4D." The speaker explains that Cinema 4D may be responsible if there is a problem with how the apparent sun goes down, and directs listeners to contact the software developers.

The audio clip consists primarily of a male speaker explaining a concept related to the sun and atmospheric layers. His tone is educational and clear, as he discusses refraction and how the sun's appearance can be altered from the ground, clarifying potential misconceptions. He emphasizes that what we see is the apparent sun and distinguishes it from the real sun's position, asserting the apparent sun is always lower while the real sun remains higher.

The clip starts with a male speaker posing a question about what makes the sun go down, with a thoughtful tone. He introduces several theories, including a particular one about atmospheric plane and perspective, and the flat earth model. He continues by saying they believe the atmosphere is much thicker, so perspective would only help a little. A quiet background music plays, consisting of a smooth, relaxing melody with piano chords and strings.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing the hypothetical movement of the sun and its appearance from an observer's perspective, suggesting a physical experiment to understand the phenomenon. He proposes an experiment with a swimming pool to examine reflection and perspective and invites collaboration to prove the concept scientifically, cautioning against considering it more than a theory. He reiterates the theoretical nature of their current attempts to prove it using a 3D program.

The audio begins with a male speaker describing how the real sun and apparent sun move in Cinema 4D, explaining that the apparent sun appears to move faster than the real sun and disappears less than 7000 miles away from the observer. Another male speaker then explains that when the apparent sun is at zero degrees, the real sun is at 35 degrees, and as the real sun rises at its normal speed, the apparent sun follows at a higher speed, getting closer until refraction is zero at 90 degrees.

A man speaks in a measured tone about a diagram he created in AutoCAD, involving real elevation angles of the sun obtained from a website. He notes how drawing the angles accurately reveals that the sun travels faster the more it moves away from the observer. As the man analyzes the distances between different points in time, such as 5:00 and 6:00 PM, he contrasts them with the speed of the spinning Earth on the Tropic of Cancer. He explains that the apparent sun doesn't travel in a straight line like the real sun, so drawing the distances linearly is just a diagram. He introduces the topic of perspective, suggesting that if perspective is the reason why the sun sets on the flat Earth, then the sun should appear to slow down as it moves away. To illustrate this concept, he uses the analogy of cars on a highway, observing that they appear to slow down as they move away from the observer.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the behavior of the sun, noting that "it doesn't happen with the sun" and that "the sun appears to travel faster" than someone moving away. He concludes that perspective isn't the only reason for the sun going down. This is followed by a synthesized sound effect, perhaps signifying a transition or sci-fi element, and then another male speaker talks about how the starfield would look if something was removed. This is accompanied by ambient music.

The audio begins with a male speaker describing that the place is the Canary Islands in Spain. He mentions a camera lens with a 122-degree field of view and states that the stars never set, their altitude is about 4,000 miles, and that this data matches what is shown in programs such as Stellarium. He speaks in a clear, somewhat technical, and informative tone. This is followed by the sound of a brief, synthesized sound effect that indicates the end of the recording.

The clip begins with someone stating they are going to replay a video and emphasizing the addition of "atmosphere or atmosplane." They then highlight how this changes the video, making star trails look like the original picture, showing "the original." Following this, music plays in a chaotic, discordant style, possibly a soundtrack or score, with prominent brass instruments. This music then transitions into a comparison, indicated by the speaker noting they will play two videos side-by-side to demonstrate the effect of "atmosplane."

The clip begins with music playing, a slow, electronic style with a pensive mood, featuring synth sounds. A male speaker then enters, stating "we can do this from any location," and explains that they all work the same. The music continues quietly in the background. A second male speaker then provides another test, referencing France and suggesting careful comparison with an original, asking for feedback on any potential mistakes. The music fades out at the end.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the sunrise and sunset in Salinas, California, and mentioning adjustments needed for height but confirming the atmospheric plane's success. The speaking tone is informative. This is followed by mellow instrumental music, featuring a keyboard and bass line, creating a relaxed atmosphere.

The audio clip begins with upbeat electronic music, setting a vibrant mood. Then a male voice speaks, introducing the video as a quick view of the stars in AutoCAD, so viewers can "understand how we draw them in Cinema 4D". The speaker describes the stars' placement and accuracy, referencing an Excel sheet with data, which is available in the description. He continues explaining the stars' view on the flat Earth with an Atmos plane, and addresses potential criticism. He highlights how adjusting the map and heights of objects can fix issues, admitting uncertainty about the actual map. The speaker states that the Atmos plane makes everything in the sky rise and set in Cinema 4D, advising people with different opinions to contact its programmers. A second male voice notes this will be the topic of the next video.

The clip begins with a man speaking in an informative tone about how the atmosphere impacted the creation of spheres, "spheres looked oblong when viewed through the refraction," and explaining how they overcame the issue. He continues by describing the moon as "a very flat sphere or almost flat, but not 100%." Finally, he encourages viewers to subscribe to his channel where more content can be found. A subtle, mellow electronic music is playing in the background throughout the speech.
